data_source: IMF World Economic Outlook via DataMapper (latest vintage, accessed October 2026)
inflation_management: Uzbekistan's inflation was chronically high under the old closed regime, 11-14% through 2006-16, reflecting the overvalued official exchange rate and administered prices. The September 2017 liberalization, which devalued the sum by roughly half and unified exchange rates, pushed inflation to 13.9% in 2017 and 17.5% in 2018; it has since moderated to a projected 8.8% in 2025 as the central bank adopted inflation targeting (2020) and tightened credibly. Dollar-term GDP fell from $97.3bn (2016) to $61.3bn (2018) on the devaluation before recovering to a projected $147.1bn in 2025. The disinflation path is real but incomplete.
debt_management: Public debt was minimal under Karimov (5-12% of GDP through 2016) because the state barely borrowed externally. Liberalization changed this: the ratio rose to 17.3% in 2017, 24.3% in 2019, and 31.9% in 2020 as the government borrowed for reforms and COVID, stabilizing at a projected 28.6% in 2025. The increase is deliberate and still moderate; most borrowing is concessional. The risk is state-enterprise and PPP contingent liabilities accumulating opaquely as the investment drive continues.

key_events.event: Karimov died after 27 years; Mirziyoyev succeeded and launched reforms.
Foreign-exchange liberalization: sum devalued ~50%, convertibility restored.
Tax reform and WTO-accession drive; Tashkent opened to investors.
COVID-19; Uzbekistan borrowed to fund health and social spending.
Karakalpakstan unrest over constitutional changes; autonomy retained.
Constitutional referendum extended presidential terms; reform momentum questioned.

outlook_next_decade: Uzbekistan's base case is 5-6% growth on reforms, demographics, and investment, with inflation converging toward target and debt staying moderate. The reform story is genuine but incomplete: state dominance, corruption, and water/energy constraints (notably the Aral Sea legacy) persist. Risks are reform reversal, regional instability, and over-borrowing for mega-projects. Analytical assessment: the most promising reform trajectory in Central Asia, but the 2017-19 momentum needs sustaining to deliver.
caveat: Outlook is an analytical assessment as of October 2026, not a forecast. 2025 figures are IMF estimates/projections.
